summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest immediate risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary determined at conception or birth, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The order also mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender," required removal of materials that promote what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces.

The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents, while existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992; the policy remains challenged in federal courts. Trans and nonbinary travellers have reported passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs.

Entry screening carries additional exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as inadmissible for fraud. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight European countries such as Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidance for their trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States following detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Facilities access is restricted at both federal and state level. Executive Order 14168 bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity. At state level, bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in 9 states and 1 territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are diverging sharply. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template, and further targeting bills are pending in other state legislatures. State driver's licence, birth-certificate and name-change rules for trans people vary, with some states permitting gender-marker changes and others prohibiting them.

Federal custody and enforcement present documented risks. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style treatment for transgender inmates, including forced hair cutting, removal of hormone medication, and substitution of psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met with beatings, solitary confinement, and reports of severe sexual abuse.

Official hostility extends to advocacy and speech. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called "radical gender ideology," describing such activists as "domestic terrorist groups." In May 2026 the White House counterterrorism strategy stated that national counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide.

Other federal orders in force or contested include Executive Order 14183 (military ban), Executive Order 14187 (describing gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," after which some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the DOJ subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full patient records under 19), Executive Order 14190 (directing law enforcement to investigate schools promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers facilitating a trans minor's social transition), and Executive Order 14201 (banning trans athletes from women's sports). Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court. In October 2025 an HHS rule proposal would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18; gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states.

Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" distributed within government health agencies, removal of words from federal agency websites including the Stonewall National Monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull federal funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people, with 11 states and 2 territories complying by November 2025.

Protection machinery remains uneven. Twenty-two states plus Washington, D.C. outlaw discrimination based on gender identity or expression, and Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) holds gender identity is included under "sex" under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for employment. Hate crimes based on gender identity are punishable federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, but only 23 states cover gender identity in state bias-motivated violence statutes. Same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015) and the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022, though recognition still varies in American Samoa and across sovereign Native American tribal nations.

A national risk assessment published 13 July 2026 flagged Idaho as the latest state designated "Do Not Travel" for trans people, bringing the total to 4 states so flagged, with the 2026 legislative season continuing to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. A separate travel guide notes there is no national sodomy law and that safety varies by state, advising travellers to check recent violence reports before travel.
tangentialFactors:
The federal posture sits within a wider state-level pattern. In 2023 more than 190 of over 470 introduced anti-LGBTQ bills were specifically anti-trans, with most passed bills focused on banning gender-affirming health care; contested areas concentrate on bathroom access, athletics, and transgender healthcare for minors. A 2025 Gallup poll found 66% of Americans supported laws requiring assigned sex at birth to be listed on government documents such as drivers' licences and passports, and 69% supported laws requiring transgender athletes to participate in sports aligned with their assigned sex at birth.

State scorecards from 2024 show the divergence a visitor may encounter crossing state lines: California, Colorado and Connecticut supported gender-marker updates on identification documents, transgender healthcare, public-accommodations non-discrimination and hate-crimes protections; Alaska supported gender-marker updates, healthcare and public accommodations but not hate-crimes protections; Arizona and Arkansas only partially supported gender-marker updates and did not support the other three; Alabama supported none of the four.

Foreign advisories about the United States are an unusual signal in trans travel risk. CNN reported in April 2025 that multiple foreign governments warn their trans citizens about travelling to the US over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens after detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Comparison points within the United States itself are limited: the country has no national sodomy law, though 12 states have still not formally repealed theirs since Lawrence v. Texas (2003) invalidated them. The FBI reports bias against sexual orientation has consistently accounted for between one-seventh and one-fifth of single-bias reported hate incidents this century.
